fullText:
Summary: Hemas Holdings PLC (HHL.N0000) is a Sri Lankan group built around everyday needs: consumer brands (Kumarika, Baby Cheramy, Atlas stationery), the country's largest pharmaceutical distributor and a drug maker (Morison), two hospitals and a small mobility arm. It is a good business: return on equity has been 15–18% for three years, debt is low and profit is steady. Last year (to March 2026) was a record, with EPS of Rs 2.98. This year started badly (April–June earnings fell 21% on Middle East cost increases) but the September quarter recovered, and half-year EPS is Rs 0.98 against Rs 1.09. At Rs 33.00 the share is 1.7x its NAV of Rs 19.22 and 11.5x trailing earnings. The methods put fair value at about Rs 24.2, so the price is about 36% above it. I'd buy at up to about Rs 20.6 and treat under Rs 18.2 as a strong buy. Watch-list material rather than a buy today.

Price and key figures
Price: Rs 33.00 (CSE closing price, 2026-11-10). Please check it live. It traded between Rs 29.50 and Rs 33.70 from April to September 2026 and ended the year to March 2026 at Rs 29.60 (Rs 24.00 low, Rs 36.70 high after the 1-for-5 split in April 2025).
Three months to 30 September 2026 (group, unaudited): revenue rose 17.0% to Rs 37.8bn, with all four sectors growing (hospitals +19%, consumer brands +18%, life sciences +16%). Gross margin fell 3.1 points to 29.7% because the group chose to absorb much of the higher fuel, freight and currency costs. Profit attributable was Rs 2.00bn, 3% lower than a year earlier but more than double the June quarter; EPS Rs 0.67 (Rs 0.69).
Six months to 30 September 2026: revenue Rs 66.6bn (up 9.5%), profit attributable Rs 2.94bn (down 9.7%), EPS Rs 0.98 (Rs 1.09). Consumer brands earnings fell 30% and life sciences 24% on margin pressure (pharma prices are regulated); hospitals rose 15% and mobility 58%. An interim dividend of Rs 0.25 has been declared.
Year to March 2026 (audited): revenue Rs 127.4bn (up 8%), profit attributable Rs 8.92bn (up 11%, a record), EPS Rs 2.98 (Rs 2.70), ROE 17.2%, NAV Rs 19.03, dividends Rs 0.95 (32% of profit). Operating cash flow Rs 11.8bn and capex Rs 2.4bn. Net cash about Rs 10bn at year end.
Twiga and cash: in August 2026 Hemas bought 75% of Twiga Stationers & Printers in Kenya for Rs 5.46bn (provisional goodwill Rs 1.40bn), with a put and call option over the remaining 25%. Together with Rs 12.3bn more tied up in stock and debtors, operating cash flow was −Rs 8.4bn for the half, and borrowings rose to Rs 25.2bn against Rs 13.3bn of cash: net debt about Rs 11.9bn, 0.2x equity.
History (split-adjusted EPS): Rs 1.22 (2016/17), 0.90, 1.13, 0.41, 1.09, 1.42, 1.43, 2.05, 2.70 and 2.98 (2025/26). ROE averaged about 13% over ten years and about 15.5% over the last five.

Methods
NAV (Rs 19.22): 1.7x.
Return on equity: 17.2% in 2025/26 and 17.7% in 2024/25; 13–14% in 2021–2023.
P/E: 11.5x trailing EPS of Rs 2.87. Year-end P/E: 9.9x (2026), 8.9x (2025), 7.9x (2024).
Dividends: Rs 0.95 for 2025/26, a 2.9% yield, about a third of profit.
Justified price to book: Rs 13.4 / 20.2 / 29.5, weighted Rs 20.0.
Residual income: Rs 12.5 / 20.6 / 32.4, weighted Rs 20.5.
P/E method: Rs 19.2 / 28.0 / 37.8, weighted Rs 27.3.
Cash-flow DCF: Rs 17.9 / 28.7 / 46.5, weighted Rs 29.0.

Hemas turns profit into cash in most years and carries little debt, so a cash-flow DCF suits it. The payout is only about a third, so a dividend model would understate it. The book-based methods are stricter: at a 15.5% cost of equity, ROE of 16% only justifies a little over book value.

Assumptions (bear / base / bull)
Cost of equity: 16.5% / 15.5% / 14.5% (a defensive, low-debt group, but exposed to currency and price controls).
Long-run ROE: 13% / 16% / 18.5%.
ROE path (residual income): 14% falling to 13% / 16% throughout / 17% rising to 18.5%.
Long-term growth: 5% / 6% / 7%.
EPS for the year to March 2027 × P/E: 2.40 × 8 / 2.80 × 10 / 3.15 × 12. Half-year EPS is Rs 0.98; the second half earned Rs 1.89 last year.
Free cash flow this year: Rs 2.0 / 2.5 / 3.0 a share (Rs 3.1 last year, but negative this half), growing 6% / 9% / 12% and fading to 5% / 6% / 7% over 10 years.
Average of the four methods: Rs 15.8 / Rs 24.4 / Rs 36.5.
Common: Sri Lankan government bonds yield about 11–12%. Payout 32%. Per-share figures use 2,996mn shares.

Fair value and buy price
Fair value: weighting 30/50/20 gives about Rs 24.2 (1.26x NAV), so Rs 33.00 is about 36% above it.
Buy price: a 15% margin of safety gives Rs 20.60, and 25% gives Rs 18.20.
Plan for 500 shares: 200 at up to Rs 24.20, 150 at up to Rs 20.60 and 150 at up to Rs 18.20. That averages about Rs 21.32, about Rs 10,660, against Rs 16,500 at Rs 33.00.
Realism: Rs 24.2 needs about a 27% fall. The share touched Rs 24.00 in 2025/26 but has held Rs 29.50–33.70 since April 2026, so it would take a weak second half or a market fall.

Sensitivity (residual income base case, Rs per share)
Cost of equity 14.5%: 17.1 / 23.9 / 30.3 for long-run ROE of 13% / 16% / 18.5%.
Cost of equity 15.5%: 15.0 / 20.6 / 25.9.
Cost of equity 16.5%: 13.3 / 18.0 / 22.5.
Rs 33 needs ROE of about 21% for many years at a 15.5% cost of equity; Hemas's best year was 17.7%.

What would change my view
Supports a higher value: ROE back above 17% once cost increases are passed on; working capital released and a return to net cash; Twiga earning well and opening East African growth; the drug regulator (NMRA) approving price increases; lower interest rates.
Supports a lower value: margins staying squeezed by fuel, freight and a weaker rupee; price controls holding pharma prices down; cash staying tied up in stock and debtors; Twiga or further acquisitions (management has earmarked over USD 100mn) earning less than their cost; leisure joint-venture losses on its dollar loans.

Business tests: 4 of 4 pass (ROE 17%, net debt 0.2x equity, profit every year, cash flow above profit over the last three years), so Hemas counts as a good business. The weak point to watch is this half-year's negative cash flow.

These are my estimates from the annual reports for the years to March 2025 and March 2026 and the interim reports to September 2026. The interim figures are unaudited, so check the price before ordering. This is analysis, not personal financial advice.
